judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's amendments to AB 572, which requires every law enforcement and prosecutorial agency to adopt a policy by January 1, 2027 governing formal interviews of an immediate family member of a person killed or seriously injured by a peace officer. Before such an interview, the officer or prosecutor must identify themselves, show identification in person, tell the family member their relative's status, and say that this is a formal interview for an investigation. The family member must be told they may bring a trusted support person and may choose whether to come to the station. These advisement duties do not apply when a reasonable officer believes delay would lose or destroy evidence or pose an imminent threat to public safety, or when the family member has already received substantially equivalent or Miranda advisements. The law also bars threats or deception — including false information, fabricated evidence, or misleading statements — to coerce an interview or in conducting one. The California State Assembly agreed to the amendments 42-22, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's amendments to AB 1071, which lets a defendant claiming that the state sought or imposed a conviction or sentence based on race, ethnicity, or national origin move for disclosure of all relevant evidence about that potential violation. It also lets a court remedy such a violation with any remedy not prohibited by another law. The California State Assembly agreed to the amendments 42-21, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's amendments to AB 2624, which extends California's address confidentiality program to people who provide immigration support services, along with their employees and volunteers, when they face threats of violence or harassment because of that work. The program, which starts on October 1, 2027, keeps a participant's home address out of responses to public records requests. The law also bars selling or trading their personal information or image online with intent to incite violence against them, and bars posting it with the specific intent that someone imminently commit a violent crime against them. The California State Assembly agreed to the amendments 59-19, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's amendments to AB 1318, an urgency measure providing that where state law points to federal tax-exempt status to decide eligibility for a state grant, service contract, or disbursement of public funds, state tax-exempt status counts as well. It also widens the definition of a qualified nonprofit organization for state refugee and immigrant service programs, which fund immigration legal services, rapid-response assistance, and resettlement help for asylees, to include nonprofits that qualify for state tax exemption. The California State Assembly agreed to the amendments 60-19, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 30, which bars a public entity that owns diesel-powered on-track rail equipment from selling, donating, or otherwise transferring it for continued use once the entity decommissions it. A transfer is allowed only if the public entity authorizes it at a public hearing and the equipment qualifies. Qualifying equipment meets one of the federal locomotive emissions tiers named in the law, produces emissions equivalent to equipment in those tiers, or has had its diesel engine removed. It passed the California State Assembly 53-22 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's amendments to AB 1037, which widens access to opioid antagonists such as naloxone. Standing orders and possession now cover any overdose, not only an opioid overdose, and anyone in a position to help a person at risk may possess one and pass it on. It removes the requirement that a person who receives or possesses an opioid antagonist be trained first. Anyone who administers one in good faith is shielded from civil damages whether or not they were trained. The California State Assembly agreed to the amendments 53-21, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's amendments to AB 858, which extends to January 1, 2027 the law requiring covered employers to tell laid-off employees about job openings they are qualified for and to offer those jobs by an order of preference. The law covers hotels, private clubs, event centers, airport hospitality and service providers, and building-services contractors for commercial buildings. It protects employees laid off for reasons related to the COVID-19 pandemic after working six months or more, and bars an employer from retaliating against a laid-off employee for trying to enforce these rights. The California State Assembly agreed to the amendments 49-19, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 763, which raises the maximum criminal fines for restraining trade under California's Cartwright Act. A corporation now faces a fine of up to $6 million, up from $1 million, and an individual up to $1 million, up from $250,000 — or a higher amount tied to the violator's gain or the victims' loss. It also adds a civil penalty of up to $1 million for each violation, assessed in a civil action brought by the Attorney General or a district attorney. It passed the California State Assembly 53-20 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 82, which limits the dispute-resolution terms of a consumer use agreement to disputes about the good, service, money, or credit that the agreement itself provides. A waiver of that limit is void and unenforceable, and the provisions are to be read liberally in favor of protecting consumers. The duties it creates add to, rather than replace, those imposed by other law. It passed the California State Assembly 55-18 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 596, which tightens how the state penalizes hospitals that break nurse-to-patient staffing ratios. It defines the on-call list a hospital must exhaust before it can escape a penalty, and says that calling nurses who are neither scheduled on call nor in the float pool for that unit and shift does not count as exhausting it. It also requires the Department of Public Health to treat violations on separate days as separate violations. It passed the California State Assembly 48-19 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's amendments to AB 1061, which narrows the historic-property exclusion that keeps housing developments and urban lot splits from fast-track ministerial approval. Instead of excluding any site inside a listed historic district, the exclusion now reaches only a contributing structure within such a district or a property individually listed or designated as a landmark. A local agency may still adopt objective standards to maintain the historical value of a district listed in the California Register of Historical Resources, and a lot split must not require demolishing or altering the structures the law names. The California State Assembly agreed to the amendments 46-18, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 73, which bars peace officers from interfering with the administration of an election and lets specified people enforce that ban through a civil action. No one may let a law enforcement agent access, disrupt, modify, or take possession of voter rosters or voter lists without a court order, except to investigate specified voting fraud. For certified voting technology the rule is stricter: access requires a court order, with no voting-fraud exception. Under either rule, agents may still provide logistical, transportation, or security support under a written agreement with the elections official. The Attorney General must issue guidance on responding to law enforcement requests to enter areas where ballots are present. The law also makes taking a package of voted ballots out of an elections official's custody a crime, and bars a vote-by-mail observer from challenging a signature the voter has already verified. It passed the California State Assembly 57-19 and became law.
